The Senate on Tuesday urged the Independent National Electoral Commission to enforce the provisions of the 2026 Electoral Act by disqualifying political candidates found to be linked to electoral violence, regardless of their party affiliations. The upper chamber also called on the Nigeria Police Force to investigate recent attacks on the convoys of political leaders, identify the perpetrators and their sponsors, and prosecute those found culpable. The resolutions followed a motion on the rising incidents of political violence, intolerance and attacks on political leaders and their supporters ahead of the 2027 general elections. The lawmakers specifically condemned attacks on the convoys of the Nigeria Democratic Congress presidential candidate, Peter Obi; his running mate, Senator Rabiu Kwankwaso; and President Bola Tinubu at the Shehu Shagari Central Mosque in Abuja last Friday. They also urged the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, to investigate the incidents and ensure that those responsible were brought to justice. The motion was sponsored by the senator representing Bauchi Central, Abdul Ningi, who warned that the growing attacks on political candidates, campaign rallies and supporters posed a threat to national security and democratic participation. Ningi also cited the reported attack on the convoy of the African Democratic Congress presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, in Sokoto State. He expressed concern that failure to investigate and prosecute the perpetrators and sponsors of political violence could encourage further attacks, deepen political divisions and threaten the peaceful conduct of the 2027 elections. Seconding the motion, Senator Ali Ndume (APC, Borno South) described the attack on Tinubu’s convoy as an embarrassment to the country. “What we need to do as a Senate is to stand up strongly against any form of violence. Last week, what happened to Mr President is not an embarrassment against the president; it is an embarrassment to Nigerians. On a Friday, in a Mosque, it is wrong,” he said. Ndume said the president’s democratic disposition had prevented a harsher response to the incident, adding that the 78 people reportedly arrested could have faced a different fate if Tinubu had a military mentality. He called on the police to restrict the carrying of dangerous objects during political campaigns and prosecute offenders. “During campaigns, the police should ban any harmful equipment; anybody who is caught with knives or sticks should be prosecuted,” he said. Ndume also proposed the establishment of special courts to handle cases of political violence during campaigns. However, Senator Kawu Sumaila (APC, Kano South) disagreed with the proposal for special courts at campaign grounds, arguing that candidates should also be held responsible when their supporters are found carrying dangerous weapons. He proposed that the Senate committees assigned to examine the matter should submit their reports within one week instead of four weeks. “I align myself with the recommendations of the motion. But it is across all parties. You see candidates with police escorts and thugs. Let the candidates be prosecuted if their supporters are found with dangerous weapons,” he said. Similarly, Senator Abba Moro (PDP, Benue South) urged security agencies to enforce existing provisions of the Electoral Act against electoral violence. “We have various sections in the Electoral Act to tackle election violence. We need to urge the security agencies to prosecute,” he said. Moro warned that failure to address political violence could discourage voters from participating in the elections and threaten the country’s democracy. “If this is not nipped in the bud, then certainly, our election and electoral process will be in danger. It will cause voter disenfranchisement; voters will be so scared even to vote; what then will become of our democracy?” he said. In his remarks, the Senate President, Godswill Akpabio, urged INEC to ensure strict enforcement of the Electoral Act, particularly provisions dealing with electoral violence. He said political candidates and their supporters should face the consequences of involvement in violence, irrespective of their political affiliations. “Any candidate or supporter caught instigating violence, then INEC has the right to disqualify. We should call the attention of INEC to the 2026 Electoral Act; no matter the political party, such a candidate should immediately be disqualified. They are embedded in the 2026 Electoral Act and require strong implementation.” Akpabio subsequently mandated the Senate Committees on National Security and Intelligence, Police Affairs, and INEC to engage relevant institutions and report to the chamber within four weeks on measures to prevent political violence and safeguard the 2027 general elections.
